title: Channelized token conveyor with proportional latency shims
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Our current prefill/decode allocator uses coarse latency tiers and opportunistic kernel hints. This leads to two recurring problems: (1) latency-sensitive small requests (interactive chat) can be delayed by throughput-oriented batches, and (2) kernel-selection signals (quantized vs fp16, sparse-attn kernels) are noisy at request arrival, causing suboptimal kernel placement and late migration costs.

Proposal: Implement a 'channelized token conveyor'—a flow-based prefill/decode scheduler that partitions live requests into parallel channels by two orthogonal signals: latency sensitivity (latency-first vs throughput-first) and kernel-affinity (estimated best kernel family based on model, seq-len, attn-density heuristics). Each channel acts like a conveyor lane with its own micro-queue, token-smoothing window, and a proportional "latency shim" budget. The shim is a tunable token/time credit allocator that deliberately adjusts throughput allowance per channel to enforce proportional latency fairness when resource pressure appears.

Key behaviors: 
- On arrival, compute light-weight lane assignment using cached model profile + initial sequence-length estimate + attn-sparsity probe.
- Assign to one of N channels (configurable, default: 4 lanes: L0 latency-high/kernel-pref, L1 latency-high/kernel-agnostic, L2 throughput/kernel-pref, L3 bulk).
- Each channel maintains a token conveyor (deque) where prefill and decode slots are coalesced into micro-batches respecting channel deadlines.
- Proportional latency shims: channels accrue and spend credits based on recent p95 latency delta to target and recent token consumption; shims temporarily throttle downstream batching or prioritize kernel fastpaths to meet latency SLOs.
- Kernel steering: use the channel's kernel-affinity score to prefer warm kernels (e.g., quantized matmul kernels) and to trigger early KV prefetching where helpful.
- Fallbacks: if preferred kernel resources are saturated, the shim redirects small-latency requests to alternate channels with guaranteed headroom or hedged decode paths.

Goals / success metrics: 
- Reduce p95 latency for interactive workloads by >=15% under 70-90% utilization compared to current allocator.
- Maintain aggregate token throughput within 5% of baseline for steady-state throughput tests.
- Decrease cross-tenant unfair p95 variance (stddev of tenant p95) by >=20% under mixed traffic.

Trade-offs and rationale: 
- Added per-channel bookkeeping and shim accounting increases scheduler complexity and memory; we mitigate by keeping lane count small and using compact integer counters.
- Channelization risks fragmentation (underfilled micro-batches). We compensate with opportunistic cross-channel fill windows for throughput lanes when latency lanes are idle.
- Kernel-affinity heuristics may mispredict; therefore we keep hedged decode fallbacks and TTL on kernel pinning to reduce migration thrash.

Plan: 
1) Design and proto: implement channel primitives + shim accounting in the scheduler core (2 sprints).
2) Unit tests for channel invariants, shim accounting, and fallback correctness (1 sprint).
3) Bench harness: synthetic mixed workload (interactive + bulk) and kernel-mix scenarios; measure latency, throughput, kernel switch counts (1 sprint).
4) Canary rollout to small fleet with telemetry (per-channel p50/p95, per-tenant p95, kernel-hotness metrics).

Rollout and observability: Add per-channel metrics: queue depth, mean token batch size, shim credits, kernel-selection counts, and hedged-fallback events. Expose channel attribution in console routes to allow per-route tuning.

Risks: 
- Misconfiguration could starve throughput lanes for long-running bulk jobs; we will include safe defaults and a global throughput floor.
- Edge cases for very large seq-len (>8k) may require bypassing channelization; those will be detected and routed to a dedicated heavy lane.

Longer-term: consider adaptive channel resizing driven by RL-style controller or workload classifier; integrate with cross-tenant pricing hints to bias kernel allocation for committed customers.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler implements channel primitives and shim accounting with feature flag
Benchmark: interactive p95 improved >=15% under 70-90% utilization compared to baseline
Throughput regression <=5% on steady-state throughput tests
Per-channel metrics emitted and visible in console (queue depth, shim credits, kernel selection counts)
Canary rollout completed with no customer SLA regressions for 2 weeks
Unit and integration tests for fallback/hedge paths added
comments: 2025-01-22 Maya Chen: Initial triage. Observed increased p95 for small requests when cluster at 80% util. Created ticket to prototype channelized approach.
2025-01-28 Arjun Patel: Spike completed — simple 2-lane prototype reduced small-request p95 under synthetic mix but caused 7% throughput loss. Noted kernel-affinity misroutes as root cause.
2025-02-03 Design review (Priya Rao): PM suggested strong telemetry for per-route tuning. UX: add visible routing attribution in console to allow ops to pin routes to latency lanes.

2025-02-05 Engineering review (Luca Moretti): Suggested proportional shims vs fixed priority to avoid starvation; flagged bookkeeping memory cost. Decision: use 32-bit counters and periodic compaction.

2025-02-09 Load test (internal/dayton cluster): Mixed traffic run (60% interactive, 40% bulk) at 85% peak util. Results: interactive p95 down 18%, throughput down 3.8%, kernel migrations reduced by 24%. Artifacts: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/ENG-531209-proto-results
2025-02-11 PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3782 — initial channel primitives + shim accounting behind feature flag. Added unit tests for credit arithmetic.

2025-02-12 Arjun Patel: Merging to canary branch tomorrow. Next: integrate per-channel metrics into console dashboard and run 2-week canary on stable fleet subset. Follow-ups: tune channel-to-kernel mapping table and experiment with 3 vs 4 lanes.
